MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I believe affects all members of this house. It has to do with the report of the speech made the night before last, appearing in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen, by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Browne) from Newfoundland. My question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I think really involves two questions, but I would like to deal with both of them while I am on my feet. This article reads in part as follows:
Tall, soft-spoken Hon. William Browne said last night Premier Smallwood's action in decertifying the international woodworkers of America in Newfoundland. and establishing a government union seems to be working out well for the loggers.
Representative of the island province, and one of two cabinet ministers without portfolio, he says the union formed by Mr. Smallwood to replace the
I.W.A. isn't the first government-formed union in the province.
The fishermen's union, set up similarly, has been successful-
"Other government-formed unions have performed well, and it's possible this will work satisfactorily' '-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext: Would the hon. member indicate what sort of privilege he is referring to before he goes too far in reading this report?

subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my privilege has to do with the statement of the minister that the union in Newfoundland is working well, as compared with the answer given in this house by the Prime Minister when he was asked whether the government is considering the disallowance of the controversial legislation in Newfoundland. I think you will agree if you will allow me to proceed, Mr. Speaker, that I am presenting a very definite question of privilege. The Prime Minister told this house when we asked him if this matter of disallowance was under consideration that the cabinet was giving consideration to the whole question. On March 10, in reply to a further question which I asked him, the Prime Minister replied:
Of course, the hon. gentleman knows that that Is a matter of government decision, and I am not going to anticipate the date of that decision.
My question of privilege is this. The Prime Minister has said the cabinet is considering the disallowance of this act, whereas the Minister without Portfolio says the act is working well. Cabinet solidarity requires that that be the position of the government-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext: The hon. member is apparently making the point that if he detects any lack of solidarity in the cabinet, that is a matter of privilege affecting the house. I do not think that is so.

subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext: My question of privilege is this. The Minister without Portfolio from Newfoundland has in fact made the statement, if this report is correct, that the government felt this legislation as passed in Newfoundland is good legislation, and therefore-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext: I am sorry. Since the hon. gentleman has said as much as he has I will give the floor to the Prime Minister in order that he may comment, if he wishes, on the alleged matter of privilege. I see nothing which affects the privileges of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext: My comment is this. The hon. gentleman appears to believe that the soundness of a question of privilege is measured by the loudness of the voice. There is, I submit, no question of privilege here. The answer that was given on the occasion to which he referred was the answer of the government with respect to the legislation. Any observation which may have been made-and I do not know anything about such an observation-has nothing to do with the question of allowance or disallowance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext: I am sorry, but the question of privilege which the hon. member has raised does not seem to me to reflect in any way on the privileges of the house or of any member of the house, and I would therefore ask him not to pursue it.

subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext:
I rise, now, on my second question of privilege. It has to do with a statement of the same hon. gentleman and a quotation in the newspaper saying that a letter was written by him to the Newfoundland minister of municipal affairs, B. J. Abbott, asking whether the Conservative government could nominate two candidates to the seven-member St. John's housing authority.
My question of privilege is based on the discussion we had in this chamber on April

Starred Questions
22 and Your Honour's ruling that a cabinet minister in this hon. member's position was not able, or would not be able, to take responsibility for official communications. I submit that within the terms of the newspaper report it would appear that the hon. gentleman in question was writing a letter which came into the hands, if not directly, then indirectly-I take it would be directly-of the minister of municipal affairs in Newfoundland, Mr. B. J. Abbott, asking whether the federal government could nominate two Conservative members of the seven-member St. John's housing authority. I believe this type of letter is not the kind of private correspondence to which Your Honour alluded the other day in making your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext: The hon. member can, of course, take what view he likes about that, but what he is asserting is that the conduct of the Minister without Portfolio from Newfoundland is in some way an infringement of the privileges of the house or of the members of the house. In my view what the minister has done does not reflect in any way on any person in this house or on anything this house has done. He is free as other hon. members are to conduct himself as he sees fit outside the house, subject to being called to account as a member of the government in accordance with our usual practice.

subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REPORTED REMARKS BY MEMBER FOR ST. JOHN'S WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the point of order you have raised I would refer Your Honour to the words you used as recorded at page 2927 of Hansard of April 22, on which occasion you said:
I take the view that the word "official" as it is used in the citation quoted by the hon. member for Laurier means official in the sense of being responsible for a department.
My point of privilege is this. I feel that if a cabinet minister with the full authority of the government can write to a province on behalf of the government, as I take it he was doing, it should be the prerogative of this house to have produced this correspondence which was written in an official capacity.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

At the conclusion of my oral answer I should like to ask permission of the house to have the answer to the second part of the question printed in Hansard, because it consists of a list of names of companies that could just as well be printed as part of my answer.
The answer to the first part of the question concerning whether 75 million acres were recently taken up in northern Canada for oil and mineral development is as follows. This activity has all been on the mainland, that is in the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon.

IMPENDING firemen's STRIKE-STATEMENT ON SETTLEMENT
On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Before putting the question may I commend the minister on the part he has taken in averting a strike against the Canadian National Railways by the brotherhood of firemen. Can the minister tell the house upon what terms the strike was averted? If this is too broad, perhaps he can tell the house upon what principles the strike was averted.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. The best way I could answer it would be to read the memorandum of agreement to the house, which covers it entirely:
Summary of discussions with representatives of the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and engine-men on the recommendations contained in the Montpetit conciliation board report:
1.	The brotherhood is prepared to accept the unanimous recommendations of the board.
2.	The brotherhood is prepared to accept in principle the recommendations of the board with respect to "arbitraries".
Clauses with respect to the amendment of the agreements to provide for the payment on a minute basis by the company for the time required for the performance of actual services shall be included in the agreements on the understanding that the schedule of increases in basic rates of pay in all classes of service, excluding locomotive engineers in Newfoundland, as given in clause 13 of letter dated April 14, 1959, addressed to Mr. W. E. Gamble, vice president, brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen, and signed by Mr. S. F. Dingle, vice president, Canadian National Railways, shall be amended as follows: 2 per cent effective April 1, 1958, 5 per cent effective May 1, 1959, 11 per cent effective August 1, 1959, 1 per cent effective April 1, 1960, except that in the case of firemen in yard service in the western region the scale of the increases shall be as follows: 2 per cent effective April 1, 1958, 71 per cent effective May 1, 1959.
It is understood that the recommendations will not apply with respect to the employment of engineers in Newfoundland. The application of arbitraries to these engineers will be negotiated without reference to the recommendation of the board as it applies to firemen.
The brotherhood is not prepared to accept the recommendation of the board on the proposal covering terminal delay. The company agrees to waive this recommendation on the understanding that the present rule respecting booking rest shall remain at 12 hours.
The brotherhood is prepared to accept the recommendations of the board on the subject of mileage regulations.
The company shall be under no obligation to hire new employees for service as firemen or helpers on diesel locomotives in freight or yard service in accordance with the recommendations of the board. When in the sole discretion of the management the requirements of the service are such that a helper is required in the operation of a diesel locomotive

in freight or yard service such helper shall be taken from the existing seniority ranks of firemen-helpers.
Firemen presently employed as shown on existing seniority lists of firemen in diesel operations in freight or yard service will be retained as firemen-helpers until death, retirement or promotion, subject to all customary rules and regulations covering the running trades and in particular those rules relating to physical fitness and discipline.
This was signed by Mr. Gamble, Mr. Donald Gordon and myself.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for sending me notice of this question, which, however, did not include some of the remarks he just made. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. May I ask the minister whether he is aware of the collision which took place last night between the steamer Prescott, I believe, and the bridge over the Beauharnois canal, which has tied up traffic? I am particularly interested because this is one of the first ships to go east on its way down to Montreal and other St. Lawrence ports. Can the minister tell the house what was the cause of the collision.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: TRAFFIC TIE-UP CAUSED BY COLLISION OF VESSEL AND BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for advising me of his intention to ask this question. I am advised that the vessel Prescott, which got into difficulty last evening in the Beauharnois canal, was cleared at 11.23 a.m. today and that no damage was suffered by the vessel or the bridge.
The failure of the lift span to rise was apparently due to the blowing of a fuse. When the captain of the vessel, having arrived at the limit of the approach, did not receive the green light he dropped anchor and the vessel came to rest across the channel in front of the bridge abutment. Officers of the St. Lawrence authority have been directed to make a complete report.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased to support the motion to refer the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to a standing committee of this house. We feel that such a committee will be able to do very useful work. We do not think that it is taking away from the House of Commons any privileges which we have. It is a well established rule, and I might say a well established custom, that when the estimates come back from the committee, where they have been discussed, further consideration is given to the estimates when they are put through parliament in the regular way.
Our objection to the government's procedure as far as committees are concerned is that very often we find it impossible to attend sittings of the house and of the various committees when they meet while the house itself is in session. In so far as this can be avoided we think it is preferable that members of parliament shall be able to attend the sittings of the House of Commons and not at times feel that they must forego attending the business in this house in order to attend one of the committees.
These departmental estimates which will be considered are very important. This is the department that relates, to a very large extent, to the great vision of which we have heard so much, and it is mainly to this department that Canadians look for action by the government to develop the Canadian north, to make certain our sovereignty over our territories is retained and strengthened and made abundantly clear to all the world. We feel that a thorough study by a committee of this house can lead to a strengthen-[Mr. Chevrier.l

ing of Canadian sovereignty over this very important part of our nation and our last remaining frontier.
This government has set itself up before the Canadian people as one which will see that Canadian sovereignty will be strengthened. That is a commendable position to take, and we are very pleased to support the minister and his department in that respect. However, there are many reports which indicate that knowledge of Canada's northland today is greatly wanting. As a matter of fact we are told by eminent scientists that Canada is not only not doing its share in developing our north, but that the knowledge which this department obtains about our north is derived in many respects from information that can be obtained in publications of the U.S.S.R.
This is a disturbing situation. I am certain that the government of Canada would get full support from the Canadian nation in taking bold steps to provide further research and exploration of our northland to make certain it is abundantly clear to all the world that we are protecting our sovereignty.
Mr. Speaker, we think under this department the government should consider implementing the recommendations of the Massey report. We think the government should act on the recommendations concerning amendments that would provide a new arrangement for the administration of our national museum. We think the whole administration of our museum is something to which this committee should give very exact and detailed attention. We feel that recent events surrounding the administration of the museum suggest that the present legal basis on which the administration of the museum rests is not satisfactory. The legal basis upon which the administration of the museum rests, as hon. members know, is merely one section in the act providing for the establishment and administration of this department itself. The section dealing with the museum reads as follows; it is to be found in chapter 4 of the statutes of Canada, 1953-54:
The minister has the control, management and administration of the national museum of Canada, and shall collect, classify and arrange for exhibition in the museum of such specimens as are necessary to afford complete and exact knowledge of the geology, mineralogy, palaeontology, archaeology, ethnology and fauna and flora of Canada.
We do not think, Mr. Speaker, that is a satisfactory legal basis for our museum. We feel that the former administration took some action, at least, that was desirable, in introducing legislation into this house.

Mr. Speaker, this is the annual motion which seeks the establishment of the committee on railways, airlines and shipping, and it does give the house an opportunity to consider in a general way, although not perhaps in a particular manner, some of the subjects which the committee will be dealing with in due course. It has been the practice in the house from time to time, on a motion such as this, to allow hon. members to speak in a general way upon the subjects which are of particular interest to the Canadian National Railways and to Trans-Canada Air Lines, and on other matters which come within the purview of either the one or the other crown corporation.
I have no intention of dealing today with other railway matters but with the permission of the house I should like to refer as briefly as I can to a number of matters which in my opinion deserve the attention of the house. I should like to begin my remarks by saying that in the motion which seeks the establishment of the committee again we see the name, "Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships." The unhappy story of the liquidation of this fleet by the government is still fresh in our minds and I must say that the amount of information we have received
29, 1959
Railways and Shipping Committee from the minister on this subject is unfortunately too little. We have received very little information about the activities of this crown corporation since it was in fact liquidated during the course of last year, other than through newspaper items. It would strike me that that is not the manner in which information of that nature should be imparted to the house. However, as the minister has stated, we shall have an opportunity in due course to examine the position of this crown corporation when the committee is established.
It is my intention today to talk about those subjects which come within the actual purview of Canadian National Railways because it seems to me that before the establishment of the committee there is a great deal to be gained by a discussion and a public examination of the facts as well as a brief scrutiny of the government's record in this connection. The first thing I should like to do is to go back to the budget speech of the Hon. Walter Harris delivered on March 14, 1957, and to remind the house of what was said by him on that occasion. His words will be found at page 2219 of Hansard of that date, and I quote:
One of the matters discussed in the Gordon report is the handicap which the Atlantic provinces have to contend with due to difficulties of transportation, and to post-war increases in railway freight rates. A good deal has been done in recent years in an effort to offset the higher costs of marketing the products of the Atlantic region caused by the long distances between the region and its markets in other parts of Canada, and to improve the means of communication within the region itself. For example, we have paid more in freight subventions so as to facilitate a greater movement of maritime coal to central Canada, and to enable maritime agriculture to obtain cheaper supplies of western feed grains. We have also spent substantial amounts for the improvement of shipping services and to meet the deficits incurred in coastal shipping.
In the view of the government we should now undertake a fresh and comprehensive examination of the entire transportation situation of the Atlantic provinces in order to determine what changes could conribute toward the economic welfare of the region. Among other questions, we should consider how best to supplement or improve some of the present means of transport in order to improve the transportation system generally. In this way it might be possible for the Atlantic region to get more value from the present level of federal expenditures in this field and from any increased funds that might become available.
I draw particular attention to the conclusion which Mr. Harris drew on that occasion.
It is therefore the government's intention to launch an immediate review of the maritime transportation problem in general, and thereafter to put forward proposals as soon as feasible.
The point I wish to make at this time is that an immediate review of the maritimes' transportation problem was initiated by the government of which I at one time was a
3160	HOUSE OF
Railways and Shipping Committee member and steps were taken forthwith after this statement in Mr. Harris' budget speech to get under way a comprehensive inquiry into the subject of transportation in the Atlantic provinces. Part of the work was to be undertaken by the management of the Canadian National Railways and part was to be done by the officials of the Department of Transport and if outside assistance should be required my understanding was that it was made quite clear that that would be obtained. It was anticipated that of necessity resort would be had to such assistance as was requisite in carrying out the study and inquiry mentioned in the budget speech in order that the examination of this subject would be carried on as efficiently and as quickly as possible.
Two years have now elapsed since the announcement was made in the house that such an inquiry was to be undertaken and despite the importance of the inquiry the investigation seems no further advanced now than when Mr. Harris made his statement in the house in 1957. Knowing the officials of the Department of Transport and the management of Canadian National Railways, I am sure that progress in this direction has been made and I can only express regret that the minister has not seen fit to take the house into his confidence and inform the house what has been done with reference to that investigation. What progress has been made? What inquiry has been undertaken? What difficulties, if any, have been encountered with respect to this matter? What solutions have been arrived at and what proposals have been submitted? Instead of doing so, the minister has passed over this important subject in silence.
I should like to give the house some general idea of what was in the mind of Mr. Harris when this proposal was advanced. In the first place, we know that Canadian National Railways provides extensive services by sea to the many outports of Newfoundland. A passing glance at any timetable of that railway is sufficient to give an idea of the extent of these services though no timetable could give any idea of their magnitude, the complexity of operation or the difficulties which must be overcome in providing this kind of service. Transportation, I need hardly tell the house, is of vital concern to Newfoundlanders and their interest in this subject as well as their hopes were raised in large measure by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself. I would remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) of the statement of the Prime Minister in St. John's, Newfoundland, on April 15, 1957, as contained in the Globe and Mail of April 16, 1957. I quote:


Newfoundland's narrow gauge railway should be converted to the standard gauge because the present line retards development, adds to the cost of transportation and therefore makes it more difficult for Newfoundland industries to compete in domestic mainland markets on the same basis as other provinces.
As the minister knows, that is a problem of extreme importance to the province of Newfoundand. I know that the minister has been there. I know he has been at Gander and has perhaps made an examination of the railway. He will understand how important this problem is to the people of Newfoundland. Has any investigation been made of the cost of transforming the narrow gauge railway to a standard gauge railway? What will the cost of that transformation be? Is it possible, either here or elsewhere, to get from the minister a statement of the progress which has been made with respect to that problem as well as in respect of the statement which was made earlier by the Prime Minister during the election campaign of 1957.
I turn now to another problem which is of extreme importance to the province of Newfoundland, namely the car ferry service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques in Newfoundland. That question is of equal importance to the province. I have no doubt that this vessel will fully live up to the expectations we had when we planned her construction. Her entry into service was frustrated by conditions which were not anticipated when the decision to build the ferry was taken. However, it is now a fact that the vessel is in operation. The vessel is in service and is operating between the two ports. For a time it operated between North Sydney and Argentia because of certain difficulties which existed at Port aux Basques. However, I have been led to believe that for the most part those difficulties have disappeared.
Nevertheless, a number of questions still arise. Is the service which the William Carson is providing now adequate? Does the accommodation which it provides fully meet all the needs of the traffic or, as many people affirm, does the traffic exceed the volume which was anticipated when the plans for her construction were made and when the William Carson was designed? Does the position of this ferry vessel meet the present needs of the island? We must remember that the construction of a vessel takes a long period of time. Plans and specifications must be prepared. These things cannot be done in a hurry, particularly for a ship such as this one which must operate during all seasons and under difficult climatic and weather conditions. I feel that these are questions which should be asked of the minister. Is the question of the

adequacy of the facilities under serious consideration at this time? Has the Canadian National Railways estimated the traffic that will be available within the next few years, let us say within the next two, three or four years, for instance; and will the William Carson be adequate to meet all the needs, actual and prospective?
I turn now to another transportation problem which affects particularly the Canadian National Railways and has to do with the services between the mainland and Prince Edward Island, in particular between Cape Tormentine and Prince Edward Island. Under the terms of the constitution it is clearly set out that transportation services must be provided by the central government. Over the years that responsibility has been fulfilled by the Department of Transport. As hon. members know, there are two ferries which operate between the mainland and Prince Edward Island. There is the Abegweit which was built some years ago-it was an up-to-date ferry at the time

and there is also an additional ferry service that has been provided by means of the Prince Nova. However, I am informed that in recent years, because of the growth of traffic, this ferry service has been outgrown and the most optimistic estimates indicate that these two services are not sufficient at the present time. Hence, one of the questions that comes immediately to mind is this. What has the government in mind having regard to the future requirements of transportation between the mainland and Prince Edward Island.
A causeway between Borden, Prince Edward Island and Cape Tormentine, New Brunswick, has been under consideration for some time. I do not want to add to the length of this discussion by putting on Hansard what was said on this subject at one time by the former minister of public works, Hon. Mr. Winters. Those who want to see it can find it at page 1020 of Hansard of February 6, 1957. Apropos of that question, let me simply say that I know the Department of Public Works has taken steps to assess the possibility of obtaining suitable rock for the building of the causeway although the results of its inquiry has not led to any final conclusion.
The subject of the causeway was mentioned at great length during two election campaigns. It was mentioned not only by those of us who support the Liberal party but by those who support the Conservative party. At a time when the present Prime Minister had no responsibility for a subject of this nature, at
29, 1959
Railways and Shipping Committee Saskatoon on May 27, 1957, referring to certain promises which the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, had made, particularly when he said that he would make no promises, he stated:
Each day in every part of Canada the magnitude of the promises is increasing . . . increases for civil servants and the armed services, a causeway across the Atlantic to Prince Edward Island . . . railroads into northern Quebec . . . improvements to Montreal harbour.
These words will be found in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of May 28, 1957.
I find that the words of the Prime Minister do not seem to indicate that he favoured the construction of the causeway, because he describes it as being "across the Atlantic to Prince Edward Island". But we well know that the position of the Prime Minister is flexible and that his attitude at Saskatoon can be flexed somewhat from the position he would take if he were speaking in Prince Edward Island. At all events, more flexibility developed in the mind of the Prime Minister because before the 1958 election campaign began he announced in Ottawa, on February 5, 1958, that the government had ordered an engineering study of the proposed causeway between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. In fact, this project was rather touted as being a positive step by the government to reduce unemployment. At all events, the announcement said that the preliminary engineering study for the causeway would cost an estimated $200,000 and that it would determine the effects of the causeway on tidal conditions and fisheries in the area. Then, in the announcement to the press, the Prime Minister described the prospective works as:
*-a great national program which will swing into action immediately and will be part of his party's national development policy promised in the general election campaign in 1957.
This statement can be found in the Montreal Star of February 5, 1958. The point I wish to make here, Mr. Speaker, is that in this budget for 1959-60 there is nothing for the causeway. It is that fact which makes it necessary that consideration be given forthwith to the whole question of providing adequate facilities for efficient means of communication between the mainland and Prince Edward Island.
If the government is really sincere in the promises which it has made about the engineering study of the causeway, surely there would have been something in the main estimates to deal with this matter so that a start can be made on the causeway without any undue delay; but nothing is to be found in the estimates for that purpose.

Railways and Shipping Committee Therefore it comes to me as a natural question, I think, to ask the minister what consideration is being given to the existing ferry services and the provision of one or more vessels to share the operation of transportation facilities with the Abegweitl
Surely the Department of Transport has this matter under study and consideration. If the position is the same as it was some years ago when I was on the other side of the house, then I have no doubt that the minister and the Canadian National Railways are receiving all kinds of representations from those who live in those provinces. Therefore it would strike me that if there is nothing in the estimates for this fiscal year to carry out the undertaking made by the government, then at least we should get some statement on the part of the minister.
I pass on now to another subject in that area, and that is the Yarmouth-Bar Harbour ferry. That was a ferry which was established some years ago and which has been put into operation. I think the minister should tell the house what success that service is obtaining. I do not speak now from the financial aspect so much as I do from the aspect of transportation. What I would like to know is what amount of traffic is developing? Has the traffic reached the estimate which was anticipated at the time the service was put into effect? Is the amount of passenger, freight and other services which were had in mind at that time developing? Are the rates conducive to the fullest use of the service? Is it really achieving the purpose which was had in mind at the time, namely that of getting for Nova Scotia a greater number of tourists? Is it bringing in new sources of revenue to Nova Scotia? And what is even more important, is the growth of the traffic which has taken place since the inauguration of this service sufficiently imposing to warrant an expansion of the service? In other words, do we need another vessel? Is it desirable to inaugurate a new service which will better meet these particular needs of transportation in Nova Scotia? I hope the minister will either now or when the special committee is formed and meets bring the house up to date on this matter.
There is another important subject, about which we have heard very little in recent months, and that is the question of the extension of existing railway facilities into Great Slave lake. Both in the 1957 and the 1958 session the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) showed what seemed to be an encouraging interest in the subject. However, the two ministers were not always


in complete harmony when they advised hon. members of the progress which was being made, and I think it is no exaggeration to say that we were left in some doubt as to the seriousness of the consideration that was being given to the planning of this project. Nearly 12 months have elapsed now since this subject was discussed, and I would hope the matter had now progressed sufficiently that we could get an informative and complete statement from the Minister of Transport who after all has something to do with this important subject and who is in charge of the provision of transportation facilities in this country.
It seems to me that the Minister of Transport should tell the house what actual progress has been made toward the development of a railway to Great Slave lake. Have the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who operate the Northern Alberta railways, made a report to the government or to the minister in connection with this project? Do they find that the traffic in prospect justifies the investment of the substantial sums of money which are involved, or do they expect the government to provide a large subsidy in order to make the project self-sustaining, in accordance with the usual practice which railroads follow in order to determine the wisdom of investing in such a project? It seems to me that the construction of a railroad at this time, if it can be justified economically, is the kind of project which would be supported by the Canadian people at a time like the present, and that the minister should take the first opportunity and the first advantage to acquaint hon. members with the government's plan.
This is not a matter simply of rising in the house and saying that the policy of the government will be made known in due course. I think it has reached the stage now where it is a matter of privilege to the hon. members of this house to know where the matter stands. No information whatever has been given, although it was mentioned in the speech from the throne in the session of 1958 and it was mentioned also from time to time in discussions in this house. It is a matter of national concern. It is a matter which falls to be determined not only by the government but by one of its crown agencies, the Canadian National Railways and the least the government can do is to give to the house a frank and straightforward statement in advising the house of the progress which is being made, if any, in respect to this proposed railway, which as the house knows has attracted a great deal of public attention.
Now I come to another matter of interest more particularly to the province which I

represent. It concerns a railway which has been discussed before in this house. I raised this matter on one occasion and I believe it was raised by other members too. Mr. Jean-Claude Lessard, a former deputy minister of transport, in a brief which was presented to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects in November of 1956, and which is contained in one of the interim reports of the royal commission, deals with the subject of transportation at some length and with great efficiency.
He divides his brief to the royal commission into many parts, but I want to deal with only a small part, that concerning railway transportation, which can be found at page 128 of the submission. On that page there are suggested to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects five possible future railway projects in the north. While I have no intention of burdening the house with all of these, there is one I would like to draw attention to, particularly the attention of the Minister of Transport, and that is the last recommendation made by Mr. Lessard concerning the construction of a line east from lac St. Jean or Murray Bay in Quebec and the possible extension of such a line to Labrador.
I have before me a map of that part of the north shore of the province of Quebec and the lac St. Jean area, and while I know that there are very often, among railway officers, two views with reference to the route which a railway should follow-perhaps that appertains here; I am not in a position to know-I think this recommendation was to the effect that the railway should follow the north shore in order to link Murray Bay with Seven Islands and then on to Labrador, so as to serve this area and the other settlements which are growing with tremendous rapidity on the north shore because of the development of natural resources.
The other alternative, and one which many railway officers seem to think is more appropriate, is that the railway should run some miles north of the gulf so that there would be two lines of settlement, one along the shore and the other inland, some miles from the shore. If the latter alternative were adopted there would then be a line going east from lac St. Jean, connecting with Seven Islands and then on to Labrador.
The point I wish to make is that I do not believe any study has yet been carried out and I refrain from putting forward any suggestions other than to bring to the attention of the house the submission which was made by Mr. Lessard at that time. I think the minister and the government would be doing Canada a service if they would conduct a
29, 1959	3163
Railways and Shipping Committee survey into the possibility of constructing a railway to assist the development of this fast-growing area.
Of course, as the minister knows, he has received many representations from people residing in the Gaspe area for the development and the extension of that railway. I remember that when I sat on the other side of the house three alternatives were under consideration. Two of them, if I remember well, were extremely costly, but one was of such nature that it could be considered by both the Canadian National Railways and the government. Whether there has been some change in that situation or not I am unable to say, but I do think that the minister should, at an appropriate time, if not in the course of this debate, be good enough to bring the house up to date as to what has transpired with reference to the railway in the Gaspe peninsula.
I should not like to conclude my remarks at this time without saying a few words in connection with the general problem of the Canadian National Railways. I doubt if ever before railways have been faced with problems of such magnitude or with such far-reaching consequences as seem to be the daily lot of Canadian and United States railroads. On the one hand they are faced with competition-extremely stiff and difficult competition on an ever-widening scale-from the trucking industry which has the advantage of being able to pick up goods quickly and to ship them to their destination with equal rapidity. This is a particularly difficult form of competition for the railways to meet, and the development of more and more first rate highways in Canada has naturally meant that competition from trucks has become increasingly sharp and more devastating in its effects on railway revenues.
At the same time, the railroads have had to meet the demands for higher wages, which, not unnaturally, have been put forward by the labour forces of the railroads in Canada, and the increases in average wages which have taken place in other fields, particularly in the durable goods industry, have made it necessary for the railroads to follow the same general pattern and to agree, unwillingly perhaps because of their own problems, to increasing what is probably the largest element in their costs of operation.
At the same time, and although the railways have modernized their equipment, the economies in operation which have resulted have to some extent been offset by increases in their fixed charges because of higher capital investment required to operate modern equipment. And all the while this process of attrition has been going on involving on the one hand the carriage of fewer
3164	HOUSE OF
Railways and Shipping Committee goods and on the other the loss of passengers to business and private automobiles.
I assume the statement I have just made has had a lot to do with the position in which the Canadian National Railways finds itself, and which is exhibited in the report for the calendar year 1958 tabled some weeks ago. The situation has unquestionably been difficult for the railways, and the situation of the Canadian National Railways is no exception; it is no exception to what railways in the United States have encountered. We have already had an opportunity to discuss the interim assistance which the house, through a subsidy measure of $20 million is going to give to the railways, but nonetheless I hope the government will lose no time in trying to get to the root of the problem which faces the industry at this time.
The Prime Minister and the minister himself has announced that we can expect soon the appointment of a royal commission to deal with this problem. This was announced, too, by the acting leader of the house some months ago. I hope the scope of this inquiry will be broad enough to cover some of these difficult problems which face the managements of the Canadian National and other railways in Canada.
I would conclude, now, by saying just one word in connection with Trans-Canada Air Lines. I know that all hon. members will take satisfaction from the fact that Trans-Canada Air Lines has again this year reported a small profit, and we shall welcome the opportunity of reviewing its activities when the committee sits. However, I would be derelict in my duty as a member of the opposition if I did not point out that the competition in transcontinental air service to be provided resulting from the decision of the air transport board allowing Canadian Pacific Air Lines to operate one transcontinental flight in each direction per day, is a long, long way from the rather rosy prospects which the minister portrayed before the last election. When in opposition he favoured outright competition and the putting to death of the sacred cow called Trans-Canada Air Lines. After he attained the position of minister of transport and a sense of responsibility was thrust upon him his words became more ambiguous but he did leave with the people of Canada the positive impression that there was to be all-out competition in air services. What has taken place is an entirely different thing. The decision to allow one flight in each direction per day certainly falls a long way short of what Canadians were led to believe.
I want to make it abundantly clear that I do not in any way criticize the decision 

of the air transport board. What I am criticizing is the positive attitude adopted by the minister in former times and the virtual complete reversal of that attitude in recent months. I suppose this is another example of the flexibility which I mentioned earlier. It certainly makes for a convenient way of dealing with problems to be so flexible in one's approach to those problems that the statements of yesterday can be forgotten as early as tomorrow.
We on this side of the house welcome the opportunity to discuss the operation of two of these crown agencies which have contributed so much to the transportation services of our country. In supporting the motion I am sure that the house will be anxious to hear the evidence which will be submitted in due course before the committee.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIRLINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point of flexibility in so far as the minister is concerned, as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) described it, has been very noticeable to us all. The only thing I would wonder about is that the hon. member for Laurier should criticize that because it just seems to indicate that perhaps the policies of the government with which he was associated were not really so bad if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) is going down the line with them.
As far as Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Trans-Canada Air Lines are concerned, I wonder if in giving this franchise to Canadian Pacific Air Lines we are not opening up the same kind of invidious comparison that has gone on through the years between the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian National Railways. Here is a case where Canadian Pacific Air Lines has been given a run on which it should be able to do very well; at least, it is a transcontinental run between major cities, which is fine. I am sure, however, that very shortly in our committee meetings when we are reviewing the operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines we will be hearing about how well Canadian Pacific Air Lines are able to do. As one reads through old committee reports one discovers those words were often used by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in opposition.
They said that if you could only compare the cost of United States Airlines with T.C.A. you would see what a white elephant or sacred cow this was. The minister himself used to make a point of that.
In recent months evidence has been coming more and more to the fore that United States Airlines are being more heavily subsidized than almost any other airlines in the

world and the number of small airlines that have been in difficulty in that country illustrates that in this form of transportation you cannot go far without some form of subsidization if the airlines are going to operate general purpose services into many communities where there is no high income available such as Canadian Pacific Air Lines is getting.
One point we need to remember is that unless Canadian Pacific Air Lines is willing to accept or is given routes that are as questionable from an economic point of view as some that Trans-Canada Air Lines has to carry it will in future appear to have a much more satisfactory economic basis than T.C.A. and we will have perpetuated in the air the very bad comparisons we have had made between the C.P.R. and C.N.R. To a certain degree the C.P.R. is hamstrung as is the C.N.R. in so far as redundant lines are concerned but not nearly so much and it has not had to accept the capital debt structure that the C.N.R. has nor has it had to accept lines such as the C.N.R. had foisted upon it when Newfoundland came into confederation. This has led to much criticism especially on the part of those people who love to prate about economic efficiency and the virtues of the free enterprise system.
The main problem so far as the railway industry is concerned is still one of the other means of transportation cutting in upon its long-held business and forcing it more and more into the position where it handles long-haul low value commodity traffic and loses out on the high value short-haul traffic. It is almost entirely losing out in the passenger service field. In fact, all the indications are that the future is extremely pessimistic and that more and more we are going to have passenger service provided on the basis of that rather damnable phrase, the public interest, rather than on the basis of economic reasoning. This is one more argument that when we set up a royal commission the terms of reference should be very broad so that inquiry will be possible into passenger service provided by other facilities that are available.
The key problem as far as employees on the Canadian National Railways are concerned is well known to me. I feel that I can speak on this subject with as much authority as anyone in the house since there are four Canadian National Railways divisional points in my constituency and two more within twenty miles. The problem is that the morale of the employees is very low at the present time. I know that the settlement of the dispute involving the firemen will be a contribution toward raising their
29, 1959
Railways and Shipping Committee morale but the whole future of railway employees is extremely indefinite.
I might remark in passing that there is one group that has never had the publicity or recognition enjoyed by other groups concerning the tremendous impact upon their phase of railroading and that is the maintenance of way employees. The running trades and the changes that are involved thereto have tended to attract much more interest. The fact is, however, that on section after section across the country these people have been pulled out of their jobs and no longer have employment. Their whole means of livelihood has been removed. They have lost their homes and the investment they had in the communities where they lived and worked. This is due to the introduction of revolutionary mechanical equipment and a whole new concept of looking after the rails. With the introduction of steel wheels in the next few years in place of what we now have there will be very few carmen across the whole system. We will have a great reduction in what are referred to as "bad order cars" that at one time gave a considerable amount of employment in divisional points across the country.
Just out of Toronto we have an indication of the effect of perhaps the most revolutionary change. That is the fact that now the brakemen and conductors on freight run through for two divisions from the Mimico yards to Capreol. This is a precursor of what is going to happen at the end of 1961 when we will have central traffic control all the way from Winnipeg to Toronto. It means there will be a tendency to run all freight crews for two divisions; in other words, for 240 or 260 miles instead of the present 125 miles.
There is also going to be a tremendous drive-and I think it will be much more embittered than the one in relation to firemen-to do away with the rearend brakemen. This will be feasible in practical terms when central traffic control is in effect and when radio communications of a standard that can be relied upon have been established between the caboose and the engine. All these factors are having a serious effect on the morale of employees of the Canadian National Railways.
Let me give one specific example. The railway divisional point at Hornepayne in my constituency is losing most of its dispatchers and quite a few of its operators. There is a whole new kind of management being introduced called area management, which is going to sit, in this case, at Capreol. These are all advances in the tremendous drive of the Canadian National Railways in the last decade to improve the efficiency of its service. For

Railways and Shipping Committee example, it is quite possible that within a couple of years the Canadian National Railways will be able to give freight service from Toronto to Winnipeg in 36 hours, which was unthinkable a short time ago.
If these moves are necessary they are all to the good; but concomitant with that you have this tremendous unrest because the employees have no conception of what their individual futures are and what the futures are of their communities. It is all very well to say that this is progress and that lots of people have been affected by the industrial revolution, and that the blacksmith has disappeared. But this is not very satisfactory to people who are committed to a line of work and have their roots down in so many communities that the railroaders have. One of the crying needs is for both railways-but especially the Canadian National Railways-to spell out their future program in terms of its effects upon personnel and upon communities and for this parliament to determine and decide what responsibility the railways have as employers in so far as those communities are concerned. Many of them, in effect, are going to fall away completely. Is there a responsibility in this particular regard?
In connection with the firemen's strike or threatened strike, one of the things that amused me was the feeling that the public right across the country has been against the firemen. This is true as a generality but it is not true in the local divisional points. I have a petition from Hornepayne which indicates that nearly every adult signed it, insisting that the firemen should be kept because those people in those communities are very conscious of what is going to happen to the communities as a result of those shifts. First, there is the shift of the firemen. Then there is the wiping out of divisional points and a drastic reduction in section forces, and future reductions in operating crews as a result of central traffic control.
It is easy enough to say that these people are being purely selfish, but this happens to be the nature of human beings. Human beings stand up and protest against something that is going to rob them of their livelihood and what they have invested in communities. We have had all kinds of examples in the federal field where the government has come to the rescue or to the partial aid of such communities and it seems to me it is about time, with the kinds of revolutions which are taking place in the railway transportation picture, that this should become an issue and of concern to the government. I am not saying that it has to be necessarily the responsibility of the government, but there needs to be some analysis of these points.

One of the frustrating things that is going to happen when we get into this committee and get talking to Mr. Gordon and Mr. Dingle and asking them questions is that they are going to say, "It does not do any good to explain to the employees what the future is. All it does is to get their backs up prematurely." Furthermore, Mr. Gordon is going to go on and say that you cannot spell out these things too completely, and certainly he is going to steer completely away from accepting any responsibility for the dislocation in so far as the railway as a corporation is concerned.
One of the things that I am most dissatisfied with in connection with the operation of the Canadian National Railways is the inability of anyone to discover what their retraining program means in terms of dislocation or of dislocated workers.
I get most scarifying reports from railway personnel. I had one yesterday about a section of track along the north line of the C.N.R. where I understand there are hundreds of rails under which there are 4-inch shims, as a result of the very hard winter we had. Every time there is a wreck, such as the one we had recently west of Sudbury, in which I understand a number of western members of parliament were marooned for many hours, the cry goes out right away, here was a broken rail. The story I have is that it was a broken rail that was not discovered. There was not proper inspection because there were not enough inspection crews going along to spot this. Most of these stories are probably untrue, but it is all a reflection of this tremendous loss of confidence on the part of the personnel of the Canadian National Railways.
On the management side, I know their feeling is that one of the things that hamstrings them in making a proper, perhaps the best kind, of arrangement in the light of changing circumstances is the very rigidity of union agreements. I know an instance where one machinist with 29 years seniority was laid off; his job is through. There are other places on the system where there are much younger men working, but he cannot take advantage of those places because the union contracts set out very definite limits where he can move, and the boundaries of the agreement under which he is employed. This sort of thing is something that calls for a tremendous amount of give and take on the part of both management and the union.
I feel that here is a place where the Canadian National Railways has to take much more initiative in the working out of better relations. In my conversation with railroaders the outstanding thing I find is that

there is a very deep suspicion of management. I think myself that much of it is unfounded and could be wiped completely away if there were franker and better relations on a continuing basis between the railways, the workers and the public as a whole who are involved in those railway communities. This is why I would hope that when this committee is working on the annual report of the Canadian National Railways we shall be able to get Mr. Gordon to say something on this point, or at least to acknowledge that this bad morale situation exists at the present time.
One cannot really see the picture of the Canadian National Railways without looking at the picture of the Canadian Pacific railway. I am sure the contrast between the two roads this year will be brought out by members of the government on the committee. It will be pointed out that last year the Canadian Pacific railway was able to pay dividends that represent roughly somewhere between 3 per cent and 5 per cent on the capital involved; whereas our government railways went $51 million in the hole.
One of the things that we really need presented much more clearly-I almost feel it is the responsibility of the Minister of Transport to do it-is some sort of separation of the Canadian Pacific railway income so that we can see more clearly at least a comparison with the Canadian National Railways. I know there are historical tables; I know the statistics put out by the dominion bureau of statistics are very thorough, but there are a number of factors in the Canadian Pacific railway setup that do not apply to the Canadian National Railways setup, and yet the accusation or the common belief is that the Canadian Pacific railway is able to do a so much better job. There is little recognition of the extra burdens and difficulties that the Canadian National Railways have.
The review given by the hon. member for Laurier on the railway problems was, I think, an excellent one. I think he could have added something which has been said here before, namely that our basic difficulty in the transportation field in Canada is that we have never been able to make up our minds as to whether we want a private enterprise kind of transportation or a public enterprise kind of transportation. We have something that is neither and yet in some people's minds it is one thing and in other people's minds it is another thing.
I only hope that by the time this kind of resolution appears in the house again we 66968-9-201
Railways and Shipping Committee shall have a royal commission report which will have looked into this whole matter of transportation and the relationship of the railways to water, road and air shipping interests and that they will have enunciated a national policy on transportation which will make much more sense than what we are doing in this particular field today.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIRLINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I have spoken about Canadian National Railways in the past I have made some critical comments, particularly with regard to the service between Toronto and Ottawa. I dealt with the matter a couple of years ago and more or less regaled the house for a while with a description of the service. Everybody seemed to enjoy it because it struck them as being absolutely correct and true. I elaborated on the matter and I got an answer from the divisional superintendent in the Ottawa papers in which he admitted that everything I said was true but went on to say that not very much could be done about it. I thought that was a very poor answer for an organization in the business of rendering a service.
However, it must also be remembered that the service I am talking about is a joint effort on the part of the C.N.R. and C.P.R. but inasmuch as C.N.R. tracks are used most of the criticism can be directed to the administration responsible for the operation of that line. I outlined the service, the type of cars and the condition of the stations, as I saw it. In fact, I called it more or less a glorified freight service. Freight service seemed to be the most important and passenger service seemed to be the least important. I also mentioned that the morale of C.N.R. employees was not as good as it might be and that there was general dissatisfaction with the administration.
Some hon. members took exception because I singled out the president of the C.N.R. for attack. I criticized the service and I related his value or worth to the company to the service that was being given. Last year I made similar comments elaborating on what I have just mentioned. I made some comments about his value to the company and what I thought he was worth. What I had to say did not go over very well with members of the opposition. May I say here that I think the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) is doing an exceptionally fine job but the president of the C.N.R. is more or less running things and the minister cannot do very much about it. I would naturally expect that the minister would have to defend his officials. The minister is giving good administration and no doubt follows the dictates of his own judgment and conscience.

Railways and Shipping Committee
I was rather surprised and amused at the reaction of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) to my remarks. The hon. member for Cartier more or less implied that I was looking for the president's job but that was the farthest thought from my mind as I have no affinity for railroading, but neither has the president. All I was trying to do was to improve the service, and since my criticism there has been a slight improvement but there is room for a lot more. More consideration should be given to the passengers and in my view if you want to make the service more profitable the first step is to give more consideration to the passengers accommodation at the terminals.
To get back to the observations made by the hon. members I mentioned, they said that I had been unfair to the president's past performance. In fact, they mentioned the very valuable services that the gentleman in question had given. They said that during the war years he did such a tremendous job that he became one of the outstanding officials in Canada and that he could never be replaced or equalled. This was a revelation to me because I always thought that the man who won the war was C. D. Howe but now I understand that the president of the C.N.R. is the man who won the war. Nonetheless, I found out that when you gouge one of the opposition's sacred cows they become quite concerned about it, but other than that they all recognized but would not admit that what I said was true.
I have not given up my determination to strive for better service between Ottawa and Toronto or any other points where the service is not up to standard. Therefore I take this opportunity to draw to the attention of members of the house again the views of these people who feel themselves aggrieved. In that regard may I say that many people commented that what I said was true and that there could not be any objection taken to it. If offering criticism from year to year will improve the service you can count on yours truly to keep on doing so until we get the service from the railways the country is entitled to.
When I referred to the salary of the president of the C.N.R. it was said that he had had another job in the United States offered to him at a tremendous increase in salary. If that was the case then it is my opinion that he was very foolish not to take it because no one in this country is indispensable and he can be replaced even from within the system itself. Having made this comment on 
the situation with regard to the service, I will let the house and the people know next year if there is any further improvement.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIRLINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one or two very brief comments to make with respect to the operation of the Canadian National Railways in so far as that railway and its potential expansion affect the constituency from which I come and the northern part of British Columbia. The C.N.R. north line runs from Jasper to its terminus at Prince Rupert through the constituencies of Skeena and Cariboo. In recent years there has been quite a bit of discussion about the extension of the railway system, not in an east-west direction, but in a north-south direction. The suggestion is that there should be an extension of railway service northwest from the present line of the C.N.R. through the northern part of British Columbia to connect with Yukon and Alaska.
The Pacific Great Eastern railway fits into this picture because there has been some discussion about the extension of this provincially owned railway into that particular region. It has been suggested that the P.G.E. itself could be extended or that service could be provided by installation of the so-called monorail system of the Wenner-Gren foundation although the latter proposal has been pretty well washed out of the picture. If it is not washed out in one sense it is at least potentially washed out because the power development on the Peace river will flood certain portions of the P.G.E. roadbed which was going to be used for the monorail system.
But if any consideration is being given, and I think it should be, to the possibility of extending railway facilities north to Alaska and the Yukon I suggest that the most logical place for the extension to start from is near the community of Hazelton which is the most northerly point on the present C.N.R. north line. A natural valley extends north from there right through to the Yukon and the whole area has been topographically surveyed. The mineral wealth is practically unknown. Forest wealth, hydroelectric power, oil and other natural resources are in abundance in the northern part of British Columbia and are practically untouched. Apart from the necessity of extending rail lines to assist in opening up the country, apart from having a north and south rail line for purposes of defence, there is the question of developing the potential mineral and industrial wealth.
The fact is that one of the largest coal deposits in Canada lies up in that part of the country. I refer to the Groundhog coal field which is estimated to have over 1 billion tons in an area of some 1,200 square miles.

This field has been untouched and would be of tremendous value not only to a railroad but to anything else in that area requiring fuel coal. It would be a tremendous impetus to the whole question of the vision that our friends opposite have in developing the north in the roads to resources program. There could easily be fitted into it a railroad to resources scheme if the C.N.R. would just get off its fanny, do some survey work and take some concrete steps towards this objective.
Before I sit down I should like to make one comment with regard to the feeling which exists among the employees of the C.N.R. towards the president of that railway. Many others in the house have made comments about this matter but I would say one thing. If there is not confidence, generally speaking, among the majority of employees in any corporation, whether it be publicly owned or privately owned, or in any organization, then there is not harmony. The majority of railway employees with whom I have spoken have relatively little confidence or faith in the present president of the Canadian National Railways. Unless that faith and that confidence are capable of being generated by or on behalf of the person who is the president of the Canadian National Railways I suggest that we are going to continue to have difficulties plaguing the internal harmony of the employees and the internal harmonious relationships between the employees and the management of the railway. I am not suggesting that, out of a clear blue sky, we should replace the person who is at present president of the Canadian National Railways, or at least do so in an out of hand way. But in so far as the employees of the railway themselves are concerned, I suggest that if you had as president of that railway someone who knew railroading, something which is necessary for efficient operation, you would have much more harmonious relationships between employees and management and among the employees themselves, something which would lead to more efficient operation of the railway.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIRLINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution provides for a study of the estimates relating to the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships and Trans-Canada Air Lines. This committee will have an opportunity to study some of the services provided by the C.N.R. in Canada. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) gave some extremely interesting and, as I thought, some factual comments on the attitude of the employees of the C.N.R. toward certain modernization procedures and so on. I should like to give my impression 66968-9-201J
Railways and Shipping Committee of the reaction of consumers or of the general public to some of the things that are being requested by the C.N.R.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this motion would be greatly improved if it were possible to have brought before this committee not only officials of the C.N.R. and T.C.A. but officials of the C.P.R. and C.P.A. There is another standing committee of this house which has the opportunity to consider a certain provision introduced by the government which will relieve some of the burden of freight rates in the country. There is no provision by which members of parliament can inquire into the operations of the Canadian Pacific railway or Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I feel that this resolution would be improved if it were expanded so that members of this committee would have an opportunity to review the general operations of transportation facilities in this country.
The railway companies of this country, the C.N.R. and C.P.R.-and my remarks now must be related to the C.N.R.-are endeavouring to remove as many station agents as possible in order, of course, to make savings for the railway companies. It may soon come about, as far as our ordinary smaller villages are concerned, that a railway agent will be as prehistoric as a dinosaur. One of the aggravating things for a member of parliament, Mr. Speaker, is to have brought to his attention a great number of requests relating to the removal of station agents about which, in ordinary circumstances, in the majority of cases he is able to do little. These applications to remove a railway station agent are taken to the board of transport commissioners and there is no opportunity for members of parliament to make any representations to the C.P.R. There is, of course, some opportunity to make certain representations to the C.N.R.
In addition to the removal of station agents in a wholesale manner-and this is particularly true in the prairie provinces-it is now reported that the railways are about to embark on a policy of the removal of certain railway trackage and the abandonment of certain railway lines. This policy has caused great concern in the communities that may be affected. If we were able, under this motion, to have brought before this committee not only the president of the C.N.R. who has been roundly criticized in the house this afternoon, but the president of the C.P.R., in order to find out why the C.P.R. is not giving essential services which I feel it is failing to give and should provide, I think it would be an advantage. I think the publicly owned system is put in a disadvantageous position by being brought into the

Railways and Shipping Committee spotlight of public scrutiny when its competitor, the C.P.R., is not obliged to appear in the same spotlight. With regard to other questions such as that of freight rates, the president of the C.N.R. is prone to follow the example set by the C.P.R. I should like to see the authority of this committee extended so that we could have brought before the committee the president of the C.P.R., the person who is giving, much more than the C.N.R., leadership in the railway associations in this country, in many instances in directions that I feel should not be followed.
There has been some discussion already this afternoon of things that should be taken into consideration by way of improvement. I have had some critical things to say about the premier of the province of Newfoundland. I want to agree with those who have said that consideration should be given by the C.N.R. to providing a standard gauge railway in the province of Newfoundland. I had the privilege of visiting that province last fall and I found a great deal of criticism being voiced with regard to the inadequate service provided by this railway. The people of that province are most anxious that the C.N.R. give to them the same kind of service as that which is provided to other provinces in our nation.
I had the opportunity also to visit Prince Edward Island. There is a unanimous complaint in that province about the type of ferry that is provided between the island and the mainland. As the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) pointed out, there are two old ferries now in service. Very often they are out of service because they are in need of repair. The people of the island were led to believe by the Conservative party that they had a program which would result in the building of a causeway. I think it is high time that the necessary inquiry be made to see whether or not a causeway is a feasible undertaking. I think that in addition to the improvement of services which would be provided for Prince Edward Island it would satisfy the very natural desire to have facilities to reach the mainland in a quick and efficient manner. The people of the island feel that to some extent they are isolated because of this inadequate service. They certainly request the government to take action in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian National Railways is forced to provide certain services that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company does not have to provide. To some extent it is unable to compete in an equitable manner with the C.P.R. The same can be said of Trans-Canada Air Lines. Although Trans-Canada has in many instances a monopoly,

nevertheless it is requested to provide services on lines which do not provide a net revenue. I would suggest that if we are to have an adequate over-all transportation policy in this country, and if members of parliament are to be given the kind of jurisdiction that should be theirs, namely that of discussing and inquiring into all railway matters, the government would be well advised to bring in an amendment to this resolution which would provide for wider scope and would give the committee authority to inquire into the whole railway system of our country as well as our airlines system.
