speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved:
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to examine and consider the Indian Act, chapter 149, R.S.C., 1952, and amendments thereto, and to suggest such amendments as they may deem advisable, with authority to investigate and report upon Indian administration in general and, in particular, on the social and economic status of the Indians;
That twenty-four members of the House of Commons, to be designated at a later date, act on behalf of the house as members of the said committee, and that Standing Order 67(1) of the House of Commons be suspended in relation thereto;
That the said committee have power to call for persons, papers and records and examine witnesses under oath; to sit while the house is sitting, and to report from time to time; and to print such papers
Indian Aci
and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee and that Standing Order 66 be suspended in relation thereto;
And that a message be sent to the Senate requesting that house to unite with this house for the above purpose, and to select, if the Senate deems advisable some of its members to act on the proposed joint committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose at this time to make any extended remarks in the introduction of this motion, because I think most members of the house are anxious to see this committee established and proceed with the work which will be given to it. However, I might just briefly trace some history which is probably well known to the members of the house, but for the purposes of the record I think it should be repeated. I might recall that in
1946	parliament appointed a joint committee of both houses to examine and consider the Indian Act and report upon Indian administration. This committee studied the various aspects of Indian affairs during the 1946,
1947	and 1948 sessions of parliament, and it completed its work with its final report in June, 1948.
Over 400 briefs were filled, and 122 witnesses, both Indian and non-Indian, were heard. It was the most exhaustive review of Indian affairs undertaken by a parliamentary committee up to that time. As a result of the recommendations of the joint committee, a complete revision of the Indian Act was carried out and a new act was passed in 1951. I think it would be true to say that the deliberations of the committee and subsequent revision of the Indian Act stimulated a great deal of interest in the affairs of Indians among people in all walks of life. Since then there has continued to be a marked awareness of, and increased interest in, the position and future of the Indians. This is a most welcome development.
Ten years have now passed since the joint committee submitted its report, and it would seem appropriate to again have a committee of both houses review the Indian Act to find out how it is working out in practice and to suggest such changes as may be deemed advisable. It would also seem desirable to have a review of Indian administration in general, and in particular the social and economic status of the Indians. The problems facing Indians in changing times are many and varied, and, I believe require periodic review and study such as can be given by a parliamentary committee. We hope we will then be in a better position to consider such measures as may be necessary to improve the welfare of the Indians and facilitate the administration of their affairs.

speechtext: On this occasion I agree completely with what the hon. lady has said, and, having said that, I think we ought to pass her motion.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amiability just expressed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) will certainly not be disturbed as far as those of us in the C.C.F. are concerned. I do not mean the feeling between the minister and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, but the feeling of amicability which we in this group share toward this proposal to set up a committee to consider Indian affairs, a proposal which, we believe, will receive the support of everybody in this house.
Ever since notice of the intention to establish such a committee was placed on the order paper on February 9 we, together with others interested, have been anxiously awaiting the time when the matter would be proceeded with. Of course, the native Indian people have been more anxious than anyone to see the committee finally set up, in the hope that solutions might be forthcoming to the many problems affecting the Indian population. I have had numerous letters from members of Indian bands in my own constituency and others in British Columbia with respect to some of the questions which they hope may be dealt with by the committee.
The minister made reference to the joint committee which was established in 1946, the committee which met in that year and in subsequent years and whose work culminated in the 1951 amendments to the Indian Act. I hope the committee which is now contemplated, or one similar to it, will have the opportunity to meet during future sessions of this parliament, because I do not think it would be possible, within what we expect will be the few short months left of this session, to complete the exhaustive study of Indian affairs which must necessarily be made, and deal with all the problems in detail. This committee could, in my opinion, make a far greater contribution toward the welfare of Indians than any other agency or group if it approaches the whole question with some imagination, as I am sure it will, and with a keen desire to find solutions to the problems presented to it.
It may be, of course, that eventually there will be no need to have an Indian Act or an Indian affairs branch. It may be a time will come when our native Indian people will be on an equal footing with non-Indians throughout the country, a time when there will be no differentiation between peoples of Indian extraction and people from any other group. In the meantime I think it would be well to indicate some specific fields of interest with

which the committee might concern itself. I should like to suggest some of these fields of interest; not in a critical way, but merely as a guide, as was done in 1946 when a similar committee was established. I should like to mention a number of topics which might well be considered in order that the committee, when it meets, may have some specific ideas concerning the people it might most profitably meet and the fields into which its inquiries can be directed.
In this regard I have an amendment to suggest to the motion. As I said earlier, I do not move it in any critical spirit or with the intention of detracting in any way from the contents of the motion which the hon. lady has put forward. The motion merely suggests that certain specific fields of interest should be included in the deliberations of the committee when it comes to examine Indian affairs. I, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin):
That the motion be amended as follows: At the end of paragraph one add the following: "including,
1.	The liability of Indians to pay taxes,
2.	The eligibility of Indians to vote at dominion elections,
3.	The operation of Indian day and residential schools and the relationship between the Indian affairs branch and other educational groups, agencies and organizations regarding the education of Indians.
4.	The relationship between the Indian affairs branch and the various provinces and municipalities,
5.	The responsibilities of, and remuneration to band councils,
6.	The relationship between the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and Indians resident in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and
7.	Any other matter or thing pertaining to the advancement of Indians which will lead to a more complete participation in all phases of society which, in the opinion of the Committee, should be dealt with.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I may now proceed; and relate some of my remarks to the amendment. The key to success in the future so far as Indians and Indian affairs are concerned is to be found in enlightenment and understanding and a mutual desire to work together for the advancement of our native population. But it is also to be found, and to an equally great extent, in the manner of our co-operation. When I use the word "cooperation" I mean it to be all-inclusive. There is little doubt that there will be cooperation between all the members of the committee which the government contemplates setting up. But you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that one of the paragraphs in the amendment I have moved, namely paragraph 4, concerns the relationship between the Indian affairs branch and the various provinces and municipalities.

The provinces and municipalities are slowly being required to play a much larger role in Indian affairs than was the case ten or 12 years ago. What I have in mind is their jurisdictional responsibility and co-operation between municipalities who experience Indian problems day to day more so than does the federal parliament or more so, let us say, than does the Indian affairs branch, and that the co-operation of these groups and elements is most necessary with the various Indian organizations-naturally provincial ones-and other agencies which are interested in and concerned with Indian affairs. The amendment which I suggest, I would reiterate, is not made in the sense that most amendments are made in, that is in the sense of being critical of something or detracting from something or being advanced in a negative way.
This amendment is designed to set out what I think should be suggestions about some of the major and important questions in relation to Indian people and to give some guidance not only to the committee but more particularly to the many Indian bands and Indian councils and the provinces and municipalities which are affected by Indian affairs and are certainly interested in them.

Indian Act

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the remarks of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) which are entirely relevant. This amendment attempts to particularize in some paragraphs the general terms of the main motion. We all realize the dangers of particularizing in these matters. By trying to particularize you sometimes restrict the operations of the committee through using specific terms because then the committee is limited to those specific terms. Therefore I think as a matter of policy and for the good of the committee the amendment is not one which should be accepted by the house.
On a point of order I would refer Your Honour to a citation in Beauchesne's 4th edition which no doubt Your Honour already has before him. I allude to citation No. 291 where Beauchesne says:
291. When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given, for the appointment of a select committee,-
Which is the case here. I continue:
a member cannot move in amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice.
As I said some of these paragraphs simply particularize the general terms of the resolution. Then too, we have reference to the relationship between Indian affairs and the department and the Indian affairs branch and various provinces and municipalities which I think is going rather farther than the terms of the resolution. We then find reference to the eligibility of Indians in relation to voting in federal elections. There is on the order paper, although I do not know where it stands, a motion to set up the elections committee of this house. I am under the impression that it is soon to be called. Certainly this is a matter pertaining to that committee. Without further elaboration I suggest that because of citation 291, and possibly because of other citations as well, the proposed amendment is out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
My concern with the proposed amendment was rather along the line that the minister has just mentioned in that it was already included in the main motion. If it is fully covered it is, of course, redundant and not needed but it does specify certain things that are perhaps additional. My concern with this amendment is that it seems to go broadly into other fields. For instance, it raises the question of the liability of Indians to pay taxes. That seems to me to be a matter of taxation policy and quite removed from the Indian Act. Then there is

Indian Act
also the question of voting. I am not sure how far that is dealt with by the Indian Act. Those items are so broadly different from the general inquiry into the Indian Act that it seems to me in the light of citation 291 which indicates that a new matter can be introduced only by notice I cannot really be disposed to accept the amendment. If the hon. member has anything to say in reply to that I shall hear him briefly.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
One comment, if I may. With respect to your reference to the liability of Indians to pay taxes I would submit there is reference in the Indian Act to the payment of taxes by native Indians and to the exemption of Indians from such payment. I submit the committee is competent to deal with this subject which falls within its jurisdiction. The subject does not wander into the other field of general taxation.
There is also reference in the Indian Act to the eligibility of Indians to vote in dominion elections. The act sets up the procedure which is connected with their liability to pay taxes. They may vote under certain circumstances but are restricted from voting under others.
I wish to make reference to citation 291. As I understood the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), he said this amendment was expanding upon the contents of the original motion and inasmuch as it did expand it would require notice. I realize I may be getting myself into another difficulty by arguing along these lines but I would submit that this amendment is not expansive of the contents of the motion itself which I say and which the minister indicated is written in the broadest possible terms and authorizes the committee to investigate into Indian administration in general and in particular into the social and economic status of the Indians.
I submit that each aspect of the contents of the amendment relates to the economic and social status of Indians in one way or another. I also submit the amendment does not expand the broad general approach set out in the motion but is rather designed to particularize some of the things which would fall within those broad general terms.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member and both ministers for their assistance on this rather novel point. Amendments usually do not take in as much territory as the proposed amendment. I think that is a difficulty which is insuperable,
I would refer also to citation 293 of Beau-chesne dealing with a motion that a select committee be appointed to examine a rise in the cost of living and an amendment that the committee be empowered to examine the

efforts of government policy in lessening agricultural production on which occasion the Speaker ruled as follows:
Though I find this amendment relevant to the main motion. I cannot yet overlook the fact that questions of policy are so complex that they should not be moved as corollaries to the appointment of such a committee as the one now proposed. It is against all parliamentary usage to refer questions of policy to a fact-finding committee.
Farther on, he says:
When an amendment is irregular in one particular, the whole of it is not admissible and must be ruled out of order.
A good part of this amendment is a repetition of the main motion, which I think would cover what the hon. member has in mind. I am concerned about the departures from the Indian Act which are involved in the question of taxation, which is not referred to this committee. I understand Indians are exempt from taxation. To ask this committee to inquire whether they should or should not be taxed while on the reserve seems to me to be outside of the scope of the motion and would require notice. Therefore, with regret I cannot accept the amendment of the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I have an amendment to move in connection with this motion. It stems from the situation in my own region. In order to examine some of the very large problems which are spelled out in the resolution, I feel that the committee will have to do a considerable amount of travelling, and in that particular aspect it will be necessary, for practical purposes, for the committee to break up into certain subcommittees. I think especially of one area with over 200 Indians which is about 350 miles north of Port Arthur, and another one about 500 miles from Port Arthur, which have very special problems. I am not suggesting that this committee will necessarily go into this type of work, or that any subcommittees will do so, but I am sure there are examples of this across the country where an intimate personal contact on the part of members of the committee will be useful.
Since citation 294 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, says that a committee does not have power

to appoint subcommittees except under special circumstances, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) an amendment to paragraph 3 by inserting after the word "power" in the first line, the following:
To appoint from its members such subcommittees as may be deemed advisable or necessary to deal with specific phases of the problem aforesaid;

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS

When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given, for the appointment of a select committee, a member cannot move in amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice.

Mr. Speaker, there are just two brief points that I should like to put on Hansard in relation to this motion to establish a committee on broadcasting. First, I would like to recall the statement made by the minister, which appears at page 4046 of Hansard of August 25, 1958, when he said this:
On behalf of the government, Mr. Speaker, I would say that if it is requested at the next session of parliament, we will shortly after the session begins set up a special committee of the house to deal with radio and broadcasting generally. All these matters can be referred to that committee, and perhaps the committee can watch the organization take shape and form and grow during the session rather than speculate, which is all we can do now concerning the operation of the bill.
These words were uttered in August of last year to the effect that if the committee was
66968-9-202
Broadcasting Committee asked for it would be established immediately. On three occasions, namely on January 26, 1959, on January 27, 1959, and on February 6, 1959 I asked that this committee be set up, the first time by putting the question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), so that certain matters which were then of an important and pertinent nature could be discussed. Always the request for the establishment of the committee was refused or put off. I do not think the house should be treated to two kinds of promises: one undertaking that is fulfilled and another undertaking that is not, and that is deemed to be fulfilled as and when the minister, the government or the other side of the house thinks it should be. I thought this should go on record so that it would be clearly shown that, notwithstanding the request made by myself and many other hon. members for the establishment of this committee to deal with certain pertinent matters, the committee was not established.
All I need say is that we welcome the establishment of this committee, but we would have felt a great deal happier had it been established a long time ago.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we look forward to this committee. We have shared the disappointment of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) that it was not got under way before this, especially in the light of those optimistic remarks made by the minister when the bill itself was before the house last year, which instituted a new system of broadcasting. I think one of the greatest disappointments of everyone interested in broadcasting and telecasting has been the very slow way in which the board of broadcast governors has got under way. I think of one point. They still have not prepared any regulations in so far as political telecasting is concerned. According to my analysis they have made no attempts-

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And have no intention of
doing so.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister says that they have no intention of doing so. Someone needs to do something about it. I know they have largely followed the old C.B.C. regulations in so far as radio political broadcasting is concerned.
One other disappointment in connection with its performance is the repetition of the C.B.C. policy, which more than one station operator has regretted, of setting out their regulations in mimeographed form, a very clumsy way. Obviously they are going to be added to on an ad hoc basis. It is a most unbusinesslike method.
I know this is not the place to make criticisms of the performance of the board

Broadcasting Committee of broadcast governors but I think that in the committee we do want to take a close look at the board, perhaps not least because of the rather equivocal position that group took with regard to calling representatives of certain radio stations before it. We had this complete flummox and misunderstanding about what the purpose of these licence hearings was and I know that in my particular region there was a great deal of misunderstanding and hard feelings consequent upon the issue of the call.
If, as was originally suggested, these stations were being summoned in a sense to account because of certain kinds of programming then it should have been stated instead of having the back-tracking in this regard that did take place because it was obvious to most observers-certainly it could be seen from the press-that these particular stations had certainly given indications as to why their programming could be condemned or reassessed in the light of the issuance of the licences.
So far as the committee is concerned, we would hope that the matter of the committee having the power to meet while the house is sitting will not be extended, as in the case of some of the other select committees, so that we will be sitting right through from nine o'clock in the morning until the report of the C.B.C., for example, has been disposed of. With the number of committees we have coming at the present time I think it would be well to limit ourselves to morning and afternoon sittings at the most.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has always been a favorite sniping target of past parliamentary committees and the amazing thing to anyone who has observed the operations of these committees is how year after year-the committee has met on the average of once every second year over a period of ten years-the conclusions reached by the committee roughly dovetailed with the report of the Massey commission and the Fowler commission that we needed this kind of institution and that there was a role for the C.B.C. in a country such as ours.
It seems to me that we will need information both from the C.B.C. and the board of broadcast governors about a most important question that has been claimed to be government policy. I refer to the matter of licences for television stations in those areas that already have C.B.C. television stations. I trust that when we get to work on the problem in the committee we will not be faced with the usual slough-off, as happens in so many committees, that this is strictly a question of government policy and that it is not for a committee of the house to become exercised about it. It seems to me that this

is the forum where we need to go into this particular question, and I certainly believe that we have to start with the position of the C.B.C. as the officers of that corporation can enunciate it from the point of view of what their position is going to be in the face of competition. Otherwise it seems to me that the government will be operating in the dark when it does come to hand out these plums, and I think that everyone agrees that in the main they are going to be plums.
I must compliment the minister with regard to his general stand on radio and television broadcasting since it has been his responsibility. One hates to draw odorous comparisons with the previous situation but it does seem to me that, compared with the previous minister, he has certainly given a little more leeway to the corporation. With regard to the board of broadcast governors, I do not know what sort of relationship he has had with them but they certainly seem to have been able to fumble and bumble along on their own which would indicate that the minister did not stick his nose into things.
Whatever relationships he may have with the committee, I hope that he will be continuously liberal in a general sense and perhaps a bit more liberal than he has been in another committee before which he has appeared where in my view he has tended to draw perhaps too sharp a line between government policy and what one may expect by way of an answer from deputy ministers.
Motion agreed to.
